Introduction

Psychoacoustics, as the name suggests, is the study of how we perceive sound. As I said in my first article, A history of acoustics: architectural acoustics, the ultimate purpose of acoustics research is to serve our sense of hearing: the ear. Sound leaves a source, travels through a medium and reaches the ear; the brain perceives it, decodes what we have heard, and sets off psychological and physiological responses. According to the World Health Organization, noise is now second only to heart disease as a threat to human health. A century of acoustics research has taught us that, beyond the obvious effects of high noise levels, the many other attributes of a sound also affect us psychologically and physiologically in all sorts of ways.

The word psychoacoustics is short for “psychological acoustics”; in Chinese, the two come out as the same term. This branch of acoustics grew out of rational inquiry into music and musical instruments, and its early history is full of giants: Pythagoras, Aristotle, Leonardo da Vinci, Galileo. Yet even standing on the shoulders of these polymaths, psychoacoustics only emerged as a discipline in the 19th century.

An average human looks without seeing, listens without hearing, touches without feeling, eats without tasting, moves without physical awareness, inhales without awareness of odour or fragrance, and talks without thinking.

— Leonardo da Vinci

I’m covering psychoacoustics in two articles:

Part 1: history

Part 2: the branches of psychoacoustics, its main concepts and applications

Anything important, interesting or promising that comes up along the way will get an article of its own. This one traces how psychoacoustics developed.

As before, I’ll follow the timeline and divide the history of psychoacoustics into five stages:

  1. Antiquity to 1860: the perception of sound and music

  2. 1860–1920: psychoacoustics takes shape

  3. 1920–1960: two great laboratories, and Zwicker

  4. 1960–present: spatial/binaural hearing

  5. 1990–present: audiology, sound quality and the brain

1. Antiquity to 1860: the perception of sound and music

Pythagoras (yes, him of the theorem everyone learns in school) was studying how the pitch of a string relates to its length some 500 years before the birth of Christ [1].

Aristotle said: sound travels by setting the air in motion.

Leonardo said: ooh, and that motion of the air seems to travel as a wave~

Galileo said nothing. He took a chisel, scraped away at a brass plate, and announced that the pitch of the sound depended on the spacing of the marks it left.

Then along came Hooke (yes, the Hooke of Hooke’s law) and declared: pitch must have something to do with the frequency of vibration! So he built an instrument, the forerunner of the Savart wheel. The principle is simple. It’s rather like holding a piece of paper against the blades of a fan: the pitch of the sound depends on how fast the fan turns.

On the theory side, psychoacoustics made no major breakthroughs before the 19th century, when two German titans of acoustics appeared. On the music side, people tuned their instruments with tuning forks and similar devices until electrical equipment and vacuum tubes came along [2].

2. 1860–1920: psychoacoustics takes shape

Psychoacoustics finally made its debut on the stage of history, and it came out swinging. Just as its name combines two roots, it grew out of two fields: psychology and acoustics.

From acoustics:

You can’t talk about any branch of acoustics without these two giants: Helmholtz and Rayleigh (see section 1, “Antiquity”, of my history of architectural acoustics).

A history of acoustics: architectural acoustics

Helmholtz studied the relationship between music and human physiology, and was the first to bring physics, physiology, acoustics and music together. Drawing on Fourier’s theory, he proposed that resonances at different places in the inner ear are what let us perceive different pitches.

Rayleigh, some 20 years his junior, then took up Helmholtz’s mantle and laid the mathematical foundations of acoustics. He also proposed that binaural hearing (more on this in a later article) is what allows us to localize sound sources.

This figure shows that sound reaches the two ears at different times. The dummy uses this time difference (strictly speaking, a temporal cue) to work out where the loudspeaker is [4]. There are other cues too, based on frequency and level; I’ll discuss them separately.

Experience binaural hearing for yourself (headphones required). Full original video: https://asmrsurgeaudio.bandcamp.com/releases

From psychology:

  • In the early 19th century, Ernst Heinrich Weber proposed the just noticeable difference (JND) in perception. Weber is known as the father of experimental psychology.

  • In 1860, Gustav Fechner published Elements of Psychophysics.

  • Wilhelm Wundt, Helmholtz’s student at Heidelberg, made major breakthroughs in experimental psychology that gained international influence [3].

With that, acoustics had its theoretical foundation, psychology had its experimental and physical foundation, and psychoacoustics was officially born.

Thanks to the great Rayleigh, binaural effects were widely discussed in the late 19th century, until Jens Blauert came along much later and brought the whole field under one roof. Meanwhile, the electrical revolution produced one “acoustic product” after another: the telephone, the telegraph, the phonograph. The vacuum triode, which could amplify signals, marked the take-off of acoustics as a discipline, and psychoacoustics was about to enter a crucial period of transition.

3. 1920–1960: two great laboratories, and Zwicker

The two laboratories: Bell Labs and the MIT Psycho-Acoustic Laboratory

Zwicker: Eberhard Zwicker of the Technical University of Munich (TUM), who brought psychoacoustics together into a complete theory and, with his student Hugo Fastl, wrote the monumental Psychoacoustics, turning the field into a discipline with both solid theory and real applications.

Bell Labs

At Bell Labs, the name to know is Harvey Fletcher, director from 1917 to 1949, who is also called the father of stereophonic sound. He made two main contributions, both in 1933: the equal-loudness contours and the critical band. The equal-loudness contours revealed that hearing is fundamentally nonlinear, while the critical band explained the subtleties of the cochlea’s auditory filtering and of auditory masking. I’ll explain both in later articles.

While reading up on Harvey Fletcher, I came across two juicy bits of gossip:

— He was the real brains behind Millikan’s oil-drop experiment, yet neither the Nobel Prize in Physics nor the experiment’s name has anything to do with him, because Millikan was his doctoral adviser. Fletcher and Millikan struck a deal: Millikan took the credit, and in return Fletcher was allowed to use the oil-drop results in his PhD thesis. The secret only came out after Fletcher’s death;

— After Millikan won the Nobel Prize in 1923, scientists found that his result, the value of the elementary charge, was not easy to reproduce. Sixty years later, it emerged that he had published the results of only 58 of his 140 experiments, because the rest deviated too much.

That’s a lot of scandal to take in. Today, it would make the trending list twice over, and I’ve already written the headlines:
— A PhD’s deathbed confession: the shocking secret of what goes on between advisers and students
— Results can’t be reproduced, scholars worldwide petition: how do you strip a dead Nobel laureate of his prize?

The Harvard laboratory

The Harvard lab has close ties to Zwicker. He spent years at Harvard’s Psycho-Acoustic Laboratory (sadly, it closed in 1962; labs close like this in Europe too, since a lab whose professor can’t find a successor may well be shut down) working alongside its director, Stanley Smith Stevens, who proposed the sone as the unit of loudness.

In 1957, Zwicker published his classic paper on the critical band (the concept Harvey Fletcher had proposed in 1933). In short: there are 24 points along the basilar membrane of the cochlea, each of which resonates most strongly at a different frequency, dividing the audible range of 20 Hz–22 kHz into 24 bands, the critical bands. The critical bands map linearly onto the dimensions of the basilar membrane but nonlinearly onto frequency. That is why hearing research works with critical bands rather than frequency: they relate more linearly to the anatomy of the cochlea. Masking, too, takes place within a single critical band.

It’s worth noting that psychoacoustics, which originated in Germany, had many links with Japan in its early days. Internationally, too, Zwicker’s psychoacoustics book was first widely recognized in Japan. Barkhausen, who proposed the phon as the unit of loudness level (yes, the Bark, the unit of critical-band rate, is named after him), spent two months lecturing in Japan in 1938 and struck up a very fruitful collaboration with Japanese researchers. At that very time, my home region of Northeast China, and indeed the whole country, lay under the heel of the Japanese occupation. When survival itself was in doubt, who had the leisure to study something like psychoacoustics? Looking at the gap today and thinking back to the ruin of those years, I can only conclude that acoustics was far from the only field whose research was set back.

Zwicker & Psychoacoustics

If you want to get into psychoacoustics, there’s no way around Psychoacoustics. It was probably the first acoustics book I ever read, because I needed it for my master’s project. There have been three editions so far, and in the prefaces to the second and third, Hugo Fastl pays tribute to his mentor. I found it very moving:

…meant as a tribute to my mentor Eberhard Zwicker, who was both an outstanding scientist and a dedicated teacher [5].

Professor Fastl was still active at the forefront of research into his eighties, and I was lucky enough to hear him speak at an international conference. They say acousticians live long lives. My boss’s boss, Heinrich Kuttruff, was still driving to the institute library at 88 to research yet another edition of his Acoustics; Leo Beranek flew to an ASA meeting in the year he turned 100. Tempted to go into acoustics yet?

But back to the story. TUM’s strength in psychoacoustics has continued right up to the current head of the field there, Bernhard Seeber. I recommend his lectures on edX (the other lectures in the course are excellent too).

https://www.edx.org/course/fundamentals-of-communication-acoustics

4. 1960–present: spatial/binaural hearing

Research on spatial hearing grew rapidly from the 1960s, thanks to Jens Blauert of Ruhr University Bochum and his landmark book [6]. Studying binaural hearing means understanding how our ears pick up sound so that it can be reproduced accurately, which matters for research on sound localization, hearing impairment, cochlear implants and more [4].

Ning Xiang, a Chinese acoustician at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, studied under Blauert. I met him once, at DAGA 2016 in Germany; after all those years, he could still give the first half of his presentation in German.

The famous head-related transfer function (HRTF) was introduced in this period, and artificial heads of every kind appeared one after another. Hi-fi fans and headphone enthusiasts will know these well, and I’ll cover them in detail in a later article.

HRTFs are essential for sound reproduction in virtual reality: a VR system has to recreate what a real ear would hear and deliver it to the listener’s ears.

Other leading researchers in binaural technology include, to name a few:

  • Armin Kohlrausch, Eindhoven University of Technology, the Netherlands

  • S. Spors, University of Rostock, Germany

  • V. Pulkki, Aalto University, Finland

  • Janina Fels, RWTH Aachen University, Germany

5. 1990–present: audiology, sound quality and the brain

Once we had a fairly complete picture of the human auditory system, attention turned increasingly to people with hearing impairment. Hearing aids and cochlear implants developed rapidly, letting many people “observe” the world with their ears once again.

A child hears their mother’s voice for the first time

Psychoacoustics has also given an enormous boost to automotive NVH, all thanks to two words: sound quality. Once interior noise levels couldn’t be pushed any lower, people found that the noise still annoyed them, because our perception is also shaped by other psychoacoustic attributes such as sharpness and roughness [5]. The character of a car’s sound draws more and more attention, as in:

— Porsche engines sound so sporty

— BMW doors close with such a classy sound

— The interior acoustics of this Opel are rubbish!

— Teslas are so quiet, so why is the engine (edit, 2019-01-18: electric drive system) so noticeable?

If these remarks sound familiar, congratulations: you’re already half a psychoacoustics expert. I’ll devote plenty of space to NVH in future articles.

So far, psychoacoustics has mostly been built on simple signals such as pure tones or white noise, while real-life sound is far more complex. Hence the rise of hearing research in complex scenes [2,7]. At the same time, scientists are no longer content with descriptive results and have begun to venture into the most familiar yet least understood territory of all, the brain, in search of the answer to the simplest of questions: how does it work? I’m confident that psychologists and neuroscientists will soon be able to tell us how we process all the sounds of a complex environment.

Afterword

I’d only just started this column and I’d already chosen hard mode: writing histories, which feels like writing a literature review… It’s been almost two weeks since I started planning this article. I’ve read a great deal of material and tried to be objective, rigorous and thorough, as if I were writing a journal paper. There are two differences. First, you, my reviewers, are far gentler than journal reviewers (which is great!). Second, I try to keep the style anything but serious, and explaining science in plain language is harder than throwing a pile of equations at you. But I enjoy it. Because I love the subject, I want to know its history; because I know its history, many things I never understood now make sense; and because more things make sense, I love it even more.

References

[1]. Blauert, Jens, and Ning Xiang. Acoustics for Engineers: Troy Lectures. Springer Science & Business Media, 2009.

[2]. Yost, William A. “Psychoacoustics: A Brief Historical Overview.” Acoustics Today 11.3 (2015): 46–53. (An American’s view)

[3]. Schick, August. “History of psychoacoustics.” Proceedings of the 18th International Congress on Acoustics (ICA), Kyoto: Acoustical Science and Technology for Quality of Life. Vol. 5. 2004. (A German’s view)

[4] Janina Fels. RWTH course: Medical Acoustics.

[5]. Zwicker, Eberhard, and Hugo Fastl. Psychoacoustics: Facts and Models. Vol. 22. Springer Science & Business Media, 2013.

[6]. Blauert, Jens. Spatial Hearing: The Psychophysics of Human Sound Localization. MIT Press, 1997.

[7]. Bregman, Albert S. Auditory Scene Analysis: The Perceptual Organization of Sound. MIT Press, 1994.
